1.title: Mechanical Waves
1.text:
Mechanical Waves

A wave is a disturbance that carries energy through matter or space without transferring matter.

Our big question for this lesson: what are some common types of waves? Grab a rope and let's make some!

A wave is a disturbance that carries energy through matter or space without carrying the matter along. The same laws you've used for particles, Newton's laws and conservation of energy, also govern waves. Water waves, sound waves, and waves on a rope or spring are mechanical waves. They travel through a physical medium, like water, air, or rope.

3.title: Transverse and Longitudinal Waves
3.text:
Transverse and Longitudinal Waves

A transverse wave disturbs the medium perpendicular to the wave's travel; a longitudinal wave disturbs it parallel to the wave's travel.

A wave pulse is a single bump that passes through a medium. In the left panel of Figure 6, a shake moves the rope up and down, but the pulse travels sideways along it. A wave that moves the medium perpendicular to its direction of travel is a transverse wave. Keep shaking at a steady rate, and you make a periodic wave.

Now grab a coiled spring toy. Squeeze a few coils together and let go, and pulses race away in both directions. This disturbance is parallel to the wave's travel, so it's a longitudinal wave. Sound is a longitudinal wave too: air molecules get squeezed together and spread apart along the wave's path.

So the difference is direction. Transverse waves wiggle the medium across their path. Longitudinal waves push it back and forth along their path.

4.title: Surface Waves and Tsunamis
4.text:
Surface Waves and Tsunamis

In a surface wave, the medium's particles move in circles, partly parallel and partly perpendicular to the wave's travel.

Sound traveling through deep water is a longitudinal wave. But waves on the surface of a lake or ocean are a mix! In a surface wave, the water particles move in circles, as in Figure 7. At the top and bottom of each circle, they move parallel to the wave's travel, like a longitudinal wave. On the sides of each circle, they move up or down, perpendicular to the wave, like a transverse wave. When these waves reach the shore, the circles get disrupted and the waves break on the beach.

On March 11, 2011, a wall of water estimated at ten meters high slammed into the east coast of Japan. It was a tsunami! A tsunami is a series of ocean waves with wavelengths that can be over 100 kilometers, periods as long as an hour, and speeds of 500 to 1000 kilometers per hour.

5.title: Amplitude and Energy
5.text:
Amplitude and Energy

A transverse wave's amplitude is the maximum distance of the wave from equilibrium.

Shake a rope gently, then shake it hard. The pulses differ like a ripple in a pond and an ocean breaker: they have different amplitudes. A transverse wave's amplitude is its maximum distance from equilibrium, as in Figure 8. It's a distance, so it's always positive. You'll learn how to measure amplitude for longitudinal waves when you study sound.

Waves are one of the many ways energy shows up at everyday scales. A wave's energy is tied to its amplitude, and a bigger amplitude takes more energy to make. Strong winds whip up bigger waves than gentle breezes. A small wave might nudge beach sand a few centimeters, but a giant wave can uproot a tree!

For waves moving at the same speed, the rate of energy transfer is proportional to the square of the amplitude. Double the amplitude, and the wave carries four times as much energy each second.

6.title: Wavelength and Wave Speed
6.text:
Wavelength and Wave Speed

Wavelength is the shortest distance between points where the wave pattern repeats itself.

Take a snapshot of a wave to see the whole thing at once. In Figure 9, the high points are crests and the low points are troughs. The shortest distance between points where the pattern repeats is the wavelength, written with the Greek letter lambda. Crests are one wavelength apart, and so are troughs.

How fast does a wave go? Find it the way you'd find a car's speed: measure how far a crest or compression moves, delta d, and divide by the time, delta t. So v equals delta d over delta t.

For most mechanical waves, except water surface waves, the speed doesn't depend on amplitude, frequency, or wavelength. Change those, and the speed stays the same! It depends only on the medium and the type of wave. Sound has its own speeds in water and in air, and temperature matters too. Sound travels faster in warm, dry air than in cool, dry air.

7.title: Phase and Period
7.text:
Phase and Period

The period of a wave is the time for one complete cycle and equals the period of its source.

Any two points on a wave that are one or more whole wavelengths apart are in phase. They have the same displacement and the same velocity. Points with opposite displacements and opposite velocities are 180 degrees out of phase, like a crest and a trough. Two particles can be anywhere from 0 to 360 degrees out of phase.

Wave speed and amplitude describe both single pulses and periodic waves, but period only applies to periodic waves. The source of a periodic wave is usually simple harmonic motion, like a pendulum, and the wave's period equals the source's period. In Figure 9, the oscillator finishes one cycle in 0.04 seconds, so T equals 0.04 seconds. Point P on the rope takes that same time to return to its starting position and velocity.

8.title: Frequency and Wavelength
8.text:
Frequency and Wavelength

The frequency of a wave equals the reciprocal of its period; the wavelength equals the velocity divided by the frequency.

A wave's frequency, f, is the number of complete oscillations a point makes each second. It's measured in hertz. One hertz is one oscillation per second, or one per second. Frequency is the reciprocal of period: f equals 1 over T. Both depend only on the source, not on the wave's speed or the medium.

You can measure wavelength directly between neighboring crests or troughs, or you can calculate it. In one period, a wave moves one wavelength, so lambda equals v times T. Since T is 1 over f, the wavelength is usually written as lambda equals v over f.

Graphs help too. A snapshot of a wave, like the left panel of Figure 10, shows the wavelength from peak to peak. A displacement versus time graph for one particle, like point P, shows the period from peak to peak.

9.title: Example Problem 3, A Sound Wave Down the Field
9.text:
Example Problem 3, A Sound Wave Down the Field

Use v equals delta d over delta t, lambda equals v over f, and T equals 1 over f.

A 192-hertz sound wave travels the length of a football field, 91.4 meters, in 0.271 seconds. Find its speed, wavelength, and period. Then find the new wavelength and period at 442 hertz.

Step one: analyze and sketch. Draw the wave with a velocity vector. Known: f equals 192 hertz, delta d equals 91.4 meters, and delta t equals 0.271 seconds. Unknown: v, lambda, and T.

Step two: solve. Speed: v equals 91.4 meters over 0.271 seconds, which is 337 meters per second. Wavelength: lambda equals 337 meters per second over 192 hertz, which is 1.76 meters. Period: T equals 1 over 192 hertz, which is 0.00521 seconds. At 442 hertz, the speed is the same, so lambda equals 337 meters per second over 442 hertz, which is 0.762 meters, and T equals 1 over 442 hertz, which is 0.00226 seconds.

Step three: evaluate. A hertz is one per second, so meters per second divided by hertz gives meters, right for wavelength. Sound in air travels about 340 meters per second, so 337 is reasonable. And 442 hertz is close to 440 hertz, the A above middle C on a piano. It checks out!

10.title: Riding the Waves
10.text:
Riding the Waves

Common waves include transverse, longitudinal, and surface waves.

So, what are some common types of waves? Transverse waves, like pulses on a rope, move the medium across their path. Longitudinal waves, like sound or pulses on a spring, push the medium back and forth along their path. And surface waves, like ocean waves, combine both, sending water in circles.

All of them carry energy without carrying matter along, and they share the same set of properties: amplitude, wavelength, speed, phase, period, and frequency.
